claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by avoiding grain-boundary embrittlement caused by thermally activated precipitation and segregation.
Controlled thermal aging that promotes grain-boundary precipitation will reduce toughness relative to the as-quenched state.
Arc melting, homogenization, and rapid quenching can yield a homogeneous, single-phase equiatomic alloy with clean grain boundaries.
Aging at 600°C increases atomic mobility sufficiently to enable diffusion-driven precipitation of secondary phases at grain boundaries.
Longer aging times will systematically increase grain-boundary precipitation or microsegregation.
Grain-boundary precipitates and microsegregation reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion produces intergranular embrittlement.
Intergranular embrittlement diminishes the alloy's ability to absorb energy during deformation and lowers overall toughness.
Prolonged aging will lower Charpy impact energy relative to the as-homogenized and quenched baseline.
Prolonged aging will reduce tensile ductility relative to the as-homogenized and quenched baseline.
The reductions in impact energy and tensile ductility will become more pronounced as aging time increases.
The proposed behavior should hold for high-entropy alloys that retain suitable phase stability at sub-critical temperatures around 600–700°C.
The proposed behavior may not hold when aging triggers wholesale phase transformations.
The proposed behavior may not hold for alloy compositions that inherently resist grain-boundary segregation.
The magnitude and critical timing of toughness loss are composition-dependent and can shift with minor processing differences.
